scenes.title: A good plan meets a skeptical room
scenes.narration: The plan is ready. The evidence ledger is organized. Yet the first person hearing the recommendation asks about delivery cost, while the second asks who benefits. Chapter Twenty-Three calls this the last-mile problem and introduces Persuasive Business Case GPT. That is a book case, not a live demonstration here. Return to the membership-service alternative from Lesson Thirteen. Imagine asking for permission to test a shorter commitment. One decision owner manages operations. Another represents the people who use the service. They need different openings, but the underlying claim and source record must remain the same. Write the decision in one sentence before adjusting the pitch. Are we asking to run a bounded test, approve a permanent model, or fund a full rollout? A polished argument can blur those requests. State the smallest actual decision. Then check the evidence column. Which facts come from observed behavior? Which costs are estimates? Which reactions were only simulated? We can tailor the order in which we present them. We cannot promote an assumption into a fact because the room prefers certainty.

scenes.title: Hold the source steady
scenes.narration: The chapter's dashboard example shows how a business case changes with the audience. It is a story in the book; we will not repeat its outcome figures as current evidence. For our fictional test, the operations pitch begins with the workload: what staff would have to record, when they would review it, and which service promise remains unchanged. The member-facing pitch begins with the experience: how a person would understand the offer, enter it, and leave without a surprise. Both versions point to the same source note and the same unknown. Neither claims that conversion will rise. Put the common evidence strip under both cards. When you rewrite a sentence, compare it line by line against that strip. If the wording becomes stronger than the record, weaken it or seek evidence. This discipline protects trust. People will disagree about which risk matters most. They should not have to wonder whether they heard two versions of the truth. The question for the pitch is simple: what must this particular person decide, and what can the source actually support?

scenes.title: Name the cost and rejected option
scenes.narration: A persuasive pitch must make the cost visible. The shorter-commitment test could require staff training, a clearer cancellation path, and a way to handle pauses. Those are possible operating requirements in our fictional exercise, not measured costs. Put them on the card before the recommendation. Add the option to keep the current model and the option to defer until the job is verified. Why test now? Because the evidence suggests a particular mismatch worth examining. Why a bounded test? Because the economics and user experience still have open questions. The book's pre-pitch workflow asks for objections before the meeting, when they can still improve the plan. It also identifies a common mistake: asking an assistant to make a weak case sound strong. Do the reverse. Ask which sentence needs a source, which cost is missing, and which stakeholder can block the test for a good reason. Then revise the proposal. If the answer is that the test cannot be run safely or fairly, say so. A decision brief is useful when it helps the group choose, including a decision to wait.

scenes.title: Rehearse objections as rehearsal
scenes.narration: A pre-pitch exercise can surface objections before the room does. Give the proposed test and its evidence to a reviewer. Ask them to challenge the weakest assumption, the delivery burden, and the risk of confusing participants. If an AI assistant produces the challenge, label it Simulation on screen. It has not spoken for operations staff or members. Turn each objection into a check with a real owner. Can the team support a pause? Ask the operator who manages enrollment. Does the offer read clearly? Test the wording with an approved participant. Would a funding partner need a different measure? Ask that partner what decision they must make. The book warns that persuasion does not replace the underlying judgment. Keep the response specific. “We have it handled” tells the room nothing. “We will review support tickets after the first cohort and stop if unresolved access questions rise” is a proposed plan that can be inspected. The precise threshold belongs in the learning plan before exposure. Rehearsal is valuable because it sharpens the next human conversation.

scenes.title: Write two sixty-second versions
scenes.narration: Draft the first sixty-second version for the operations owner. Name the decision, the delivery change, the review date, and what would stop the test. Draft the second for the person accountable to members. Name the job, the proposed experience, the consent boundary, and what remains unverified. These are two ways into one decision. Do not write a promise that the evidence cannot carry. Annotate each claim with the source ID or mark it assumption. Where a source is absent, change the sentence to a question. Read both versions aloud. The first should sound like someone who has considered the work of implementation. The second should sound like someone who respects the burden of trying a new service. Neither should hide a condition in fine print. If the two versions lead listeners to different decisions, the pitch has drifted. Bring them back to the same bounded request. A source-linked brief lets someone disagree with your recommendation while still trusting your account of the facts.

scenes.title: Make the decision file usable
scenes.narration: Pause here. Put both pitch versions into the decision file. Under each, list the claims, their exact source IDs, and one objection you still need a person to answer. Add the decision requested, the rejected alternative, the cost, the owner, and the review date. Resume when you can answer this question: what observation would make you change your recommendation? If you cannot answer, the argument is still a defense of a preferred story. Keep private deal terms, customer records, and internal conversations inside approved systems; this exercise uses a fictional proposal. Persuasive GPT remains a named book case. We have created an editorial teaching card, not proof of a deployed tool or a successful pitch. The next lesson asks what happens after one team learns from a test and other teams want to repeat it. Save the source strip. At scale, the same evidence will need to survive more meetings, more owners, and more chances for its meaning to drift.
